set1.q: Which organism belongs to the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex rather than to the nontuberculous mycobacteria?
opts: Mycobacterium abscessus is a nontuberculous mycobacterium, one of the other pathogens of nontuberculous lung disease besides Mycobacterium avium complex. Tell: it sits with avium and kansasii, not with bovis.

Correct. The Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex causes tuberculosis. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is its principal human pathogen, and the other members named are Mycobacterium bovis and Mycobacterium africanum.

Mycobacterium avium complex is a nontuberculous mycobacterium and a common cause of nontuberculous lung disease. Tell: the tuberculosis complex members named are Mycobacterium tuberculosis, bovis and africanum.

set1.q: Which finding places a person in the 5 mm tuberculin skin test induration group?
opts: Increased exposure risk belongs to the 10 mm group. Tell: the 5 mm group is the highest-risk tier, such as a recent close contact.
A person with no known risk factors needs 15 mm or more to be positive. Tell: lowest risk, highest cut-off.

Correct. The 5 mm group is human immunodeficiency virus infection, recent close contact, transplant, major immunosuppression, or imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. These people get the lowest cut-off because their risk is highest.
Work in a congregate care setting
Work in a high-risk congregate setting places a person in the 10 mm group. Tell: 5 mm is reserved for immunosuppression, recent close contact and imaging suggesting old tuberculosis.

set1.q: Which situation can cause a false-negative tuberculin skin test?
opts: After treatment, the skin test and blood assay may stay positive, so prior treatment does not create a false negative. Tell: treated disease leaves a positive test; immunosuppression hides one.

Correct. Immunosuppression or severe tuberculosis may cause false negatives, and early infection can also give a negative result. That is why symptoms or high clinical suspicion require disease evaluation now, whatever the skin test shows.
BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccination causes false-positive skin tests, not false negatives. Tell: vaccine and nontuberculous exposure push the test up; immunosuppression pulls it down.
Some nontuberculous mycobacterial exposures cause a false-positive skin test. Tell: they make the test read positive without tuberculosis infection, the opposite error.

set1.q: In tuberculosis, what does massive hematogenous dissemination produce?
opts: Correct. Massive hematogenous dissemination, from progressive primary or progressive secondary disease, produces miliary tuberculosis, with tiny lesions seeded through organs such as the liver and spleen. On imaging, miliary disease can produce diffuse tiny nodules.
A healed lesion is a scar in which the organisms are no longer viable, the outcome when the immune response wins. Tell: dissemination is the opposite of healing.
Latent lesions hold dormant organisms, pulmonary or extrapulmonary, without disease. Tell: latency is a contained state; massive dissemination through the blood is uncontained disease.
The primary complex is the first, localized focus of caseation with its lymph node, at the start of infection. Tell: spread through the bloodstream to many organs is the miliary form.

set1.q: In the standard regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis, which drugs continue for the final 4 months?
opts: Ethambutol belongs to the first 2 months and can stop once susceptibility to isoniazid and rifampin is established. Tell: the 4-month phase is isoniazid with rifampin.
Pyrazinamide is given only in the initial 2-month phase with the other three drugs. Tell: the continuation phase drops pyrazinamide and keeps isoniazid and rifampin.
Pyrazinamide and ethambutol are both limited to the initial phase. Tell: the drugs that carry on for 4 months are isoniazid and rifampin.

Correct. After 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, isoniazid and rifampin continue for 4 more months, for 6 months in all. Daily therapy with directly observed therapy, in person or by video, supports completion.

set1.q: Which regimen treats macrolide-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease?
opts: Inhaled liposomal amikacin is considered when cultures stay positive after 6 months or more of treatment, not as initial therapy. Tell: start with azithromycin, ethambutol and a rifamycin.

Correct. Macrolide-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease is treated with azithromycin, ethambutol and a rifamycin, under specialist direction, for at least 12 months after culture conversion.
Isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide are tuberculosis drugs, given with ethambutol in the standard initial phase. Tell: avium complex disease is treated around a macrolide, azithromycin.
Isoniazid, rifapentine and moxifloxacin form the last 9 weeks of the 17-week tuberculosis regimen. Tell: avium complex treatment uses azithromycin, ethambutol and a rifamycin.

set1.q: At what point in tuberculosis treatment is the response documented?
opts: One month is the interval for reviewing adherence, symptoms and adverse effects, not the documented response point. Tell: response is recorded at 2 months.

Correct. Sputum cultures are followed until conversion and the response is documented at 2 months, the end of the initial phase. Adherence, symptoms and adverse effects are reviewed at least monthly throughout.
Four months is the length of the continuation phase of the standard regimen, not when response is documented. Tell: response is documented at 2 months.
Six months is the full standard regimen, far too late to first document a response. Tell: the checkpoint is 2 months.

set1.q: What does the chest radiograph usually show in latent tuberculosis infection?
opts: Diffuse tiny nodules are miliary disease, the result of hematogenous dissemination. Tell: latent infection is contained and usually shows a normal film.

Correct. Latent tuberculosis infection usually has a normal chest radiograph. By definition there is no evidence of disease after clinical evaluation, which includes chest imaging after a positive skin test or blood assay.
Upper-lobe disease that may cavitate is post-primary tuberculosis, active disease. Tell: latent infection usually leaves the film normal.
Hilar or mediastinal adenopathy, infiltrates or effusion fit primary disease. Tell: latency has no evidence of disease, so the radiograph is usually normal.

set1.q: Which chest film pattern is typical of post-primary tuberculosis?
opts: Latent tuberculosis infection usually has a normal chest radiograph. Tell: post-primary disease shows upper-lobe involvement, often with cavities.
Diffuse tiny nodules are miliary disease, from hematogenous dissemination. Tell: post-primary disease is upper-lobe and cavitary.

Correct. Post-primary disease often involves the upper lobes and may cavitate. Primary disease may show hilar or mediastinal adenopathy, infiltrates or effusion, and the patterns overlap, so the film cannot time the infection.
Hilar or mediastinal adenopathy, infiltrates or effusion are the primary disease pattern. Tell: post-primary disease favors the upper lobes and cavitation.

set1.q: Besides compatible symptoms, compatible imaging and microbiology, which domain is required to diagnose nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease?
opts: Cavitation on a plain chest film

Imaging must be compatible, and computed tomography may show nodular bronchiectasis or fibrocavitary disease, but cavitation is not itself a required domain. Tell: the remaining domain is exclusion of alternative diagnoses.
Person-to-person spread is uncommon, so exposure to a case is not a criterion. Tell: the remaining domain is exclusion of alternative diagnoses.
Correct. Diagnosis requires all domains: compatible symptoms and imaging, exclusion of alternative diagnoses, and the microbiologic criterion, usually 2 or more sputum cultures of the same species.
Positive skin test and blood assay
The skin test and blood assay detect tuberculosis infection and play no part in the nontuberculous criteria. Tell: the remaining domain is exclusion of alternative diagnoses.

set1.q: Who is eligible for the 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen?
opts: Age 12 or older with susceptible disease
Correct. The 17-week rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen is for patients aged 12 or older with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis. Eligibility, interactions and disease site require expert review.
Rifampin resistance requires rapid susceptibility testing and expert management; the 17-week regimen is for susceptible disease in patients 12 or older. Tell: susceptible, not resistant.
The shortened option for children is for selected children with nonsevere disease, and the 17-week regimen starts at age 12. Tell: severe disease in a young child is not a short-course candidate.
Latent infection has its own short regimens, such as weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months. Tell: the 17-week regimen treats susceptible pulmonary disease.

set1.q: After a positive tuberculin skin test, what separates latent infection from tuberculosis disease?
opts: Induration is read against risk-based cut-offs to decide whether the test is positive; it shows infection, not whether disease is present. Tell: size decides positive or negative, not latent or active.

The interferon-gamma release assay also detects an immune response to infection, so it cannot separate latent infection from disease either. Tell: neither the skin test nor the blood test sorts latent from active.
A repeat skin test in 8 weeks

Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is for an early negative result in a recent contact, not for sorting a positive one. Tell: a positive result goes to clinical evaluation and imaging.

Correct. Neither the skin test nor the interferon-gamma release assay distinguishes latent infection from disease, so a positive result requires clinical evaluation and chest imaging; symptoms or suspicious imaging then require microbiologic testing.

set1.q: Which check is listed before choosing a latent tuberculosis infection regimen?
opts: Culture conversion is followed during treatment of disease, and it starts the 12-month clock in Mycobacterium avium complex disease. Tell: latent infection has no sputum to convert.

Induration is read once, at 48 to 72 hours, against risk-based cut-offs, and the skin test may stay positive after treatment. Tell: the latent checks are interactions, pregnancy and source-case resistance.
Response at 2 months is documented in treatment of disease, not in choosing a latent regimen. Tell: before latent treatment, check interactions, pregnancy and the source case's resistance.

Correct. Before a latent regimen is chosen, drug interactions, pregnancy considerations and source-case resistance are checked, and tuberculosis disease is excluded. A source case's resistance can make a regimen ineffective.

set1.q: How far apart are the sputum specimens for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis collected?
opts: One to 2 hours apart is too close together; the specimens are spaced 8 to 24 hours apart and one must be early-morning. Tell: the spacing is 8 to 24 hours.
Four to 6 hours is shorter than the required spacing of 8 to 24 hours. Tell: the minimum gap is 8 hours.

Correct. The three sputum specimens are collected 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early-morning specimen, and sent for acid-fast smear, mycobacterial culture and, on at least one, a rapid molecular test.
Forty-eight to 72 hours is when a tuberculin skin test is read, not the sputum spacing. Tell: sputum is 8 to 24 hours apart; the skin test is read at 48 to 72.

set1.q: When is the local or state tuberculosis program notified?
opts: Rifampin resistance calls for rapid susceptibility testing and expert management, but notification is required for any presumed or confirmed disease. Tell: drug resistance is not the trigger for reporting.

Correct. Immediate management of pulmonary tuberculosis starts with notifying the local or state tuberculosis program of presumed or confirmed disease, alongside airborne isolation when indicated and fit-tested N95 or higher respiratory protection for staff.
Waiting for culture would delay reporting by weeks, because cultures grow slowly; presumed disease is reported too. Tell: the program hears about presumed cases, not just confirmed ones.
Notification is part of immediate management, at the start, so contacts and treatment can be coordinated. Tell: report at presumption or confirmation, not at the end of therapy.

set1.q: After a recent tuberculosis exposure, a first tuberculin skin test is negative. When is the test repeated?
opts: Two to 4 weeks may still be too early: early infection can produce a negative result, and the repeat is set at 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure. Tell: the repeat window is 8 to 10 weeks.
Four to 6 weeks falls short of the repeat window of 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure. Tell: the immune response needs time; wait 8 to 10 weeks.

Correct. Early infection can produce a negative skin test or blood assay, so testing is repeated 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure when indicated. Symptoms or high clinical suspicion still require disease evaluation now.
Sixteen to 20 weeks is later than needed; the repeat is 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure. Tell: the window is 8 to 10 weeks, not months later.

set1.q: Which endemic fungal infection is named on the differential for pulmonary tuberculosis?
opts: Pneumocystis is not the endemic fungal infection named on the tuberculosis differential; histoplasmosis is. Tell: the endemic fungal infection listed is histoplasmosis.
Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease is on the tuberculosis differential, but it is mycobacterial, not fungal. Tell: the endemic fungal infection named there is histoplasmosis.
Candidiasis is not on the pulmonary tuberculosis differential. Tell: the endemic fungal infection listed is histoplasmosis, beside chronic pulmonary aspergillosis.

Correct. Endemic fungal infection, including histoplasmosis, is on the pulmonary tuberculosis differential, with nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, bacterial pneumonia or lung abscess, bronchiectasis or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, and lung cancer.

set1.q: During evaluation of suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, which test is offered when the patient's status for a coexisting infection that raises progression risk is unknown?
opts: A repeat skin test 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is for a contact with an early negative result, not part of evaluating suspected disease. Tell: suspected disease needs microbiology, and an unknown status needs the virus test.
Computed tomography can clarify findings or complications when needed; it is not routine. Tell: the test offered to every patient of unknown status is the human immunodeficiency virus test.

Neither blood assay nor skin test distinguishes latent infection from disease, and symptoms require microbiology even when they are negative. Tell: the status test that is offered concerns human immunodeficiency virus.

Correct. The microbiologic evaluation of suspected pulmonary tuberculosis includes offering human immunodeficiency virus testing when status is unknown, alongside sputum smear, culture, molecular and drug-susceptibility testing.

set1.q: Which respiratory protection do staff use when caring for a patient with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis?
opts: Patient source control is used during transport, in addition to staff respiratory protection, not instead of it. Tell: staff wear fit-tested N95 or higher themselves.
Gloves and gowns do not protect against airborne aerosols; staff need fit-tested N95 or higher respiratory protection. Tell: tuberculosis spreads through the air, so protection is respiratory.

Correct. Staff use fit-tested N95 or higher-level respiratory protection, the patient is placed in an airborne infection isolation room when indicated, and the patient uses source control during transport.
No mask once therapy has begun

Isolation ends through clinical, laboratory and public-health criteria, not after a fixed treatment interval, so starting therapy does not end staff protection. Tell: criteria, not the first dose, end precautions.

set1.q: How are most nontuberculous mycobacterial infections acquired?
opts: Reactivation of a dormant focus describes secondary tuberculosis. Tell: nontuberculous infection mostly comes in from the environment.
Reinfection from another person is a tuberculosis concept; nontuberculous mycobacteria rarely pass between people. Tell: think environment, not household.

Correct. Most nontuberculous mycobacterial infections arise from environmental exposure, and person-to-person spread is uncommon. These are environmental mycobacteria with both slow and rapid growers.

Airborne spread from a person with pulmonary or laryngeal disease is how tuberculosis travels; with nontuberculous mycobacteria person-to-person spread is uncommon. Tell: these organisms come from the environment.

set1.q: Which description fits Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
opts: Principal human pathogen of its complex

Correct. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the principal human pathogen of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, the group that causes tuberculosis. It is a slow-growing acid-fast bacillus whose cultures can take weeks.

Environmental species with both slow and rapid growers are the nontuberculous mycobacteria. Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly. Tell: environment and rapid growth point to the nontuberculous group.
Acquired mainly from soil and water

Environmental exposure is how most nontuberculous mycobacterial infections arise. Tuberculosis spreads through the air from people with pulmonary or laryngeal disease. Tell: tuberculosis comes from a person, not from the environment.
Organism with no detectable cell wall
Mycobacteria are acid-fast bacilli precisely because they have lipid-rich cell walls containing mycolic acids. Tell: the mycolic acid wall is what makes the smear stain acid-fast.

set1.q: What does a normal physical examination mean in suspected pulmonary tuberculosis?
opts: Examination has limited sensitivity, so a normal examination cannot exclude pulmonary tuberculosis. Symptoms, risk history, imaging and microbiology guide the evaluation. Tell: a normal chest exam is common in this disease.

Latent infection is defined by no evidence of disease after a full clinical evaluation, including imaging, not by a normal examination alone. Tell: examination is too insensitive to sort latent from active.
It means the patient is not infectious
Infectiousness depends on pulmonary or laryngeal disease releasing aerosols, which a normal examination does not rule out. Tell: a quiet chest can still belong to an infectious patient.
It does not exclude the disease

Correct. Physical examination has limited sensitivity in pulmonary tuberculosis. Findings may include crackles or bronchial breath sounds, and fever, wasting or lymphadenopathy can give clues, but a normal examination does not exclude the disease.

set1.q: Which history is an exposure risk for tuberculosis rather than a progression risk?
opts: Diabetes mellitus is an additional risk factor for progression from infection to disease, not a way of being exposed. Tell: exposure risks describe contact with the organism; diabetes describes the host.
Prolonged corticosteroid therapy is a higher progression risk, with tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and transplantation. Tell: drugs that weaken immunity change progression, not exposure.
Chronic kidney disease or dialysis is an additional progression risk factor. Tell: exposure risks are about where a person has been and whom they shared air with.

Correct. Exposure risks are close contact with infectious tuberculosis, prolonged exposure in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces, residence or work in settings with ongoing transmission, and travel or residence in areas with high incidence.

set1.q: Which contacts of an infectious tuberculosis case need prompt public-health assessment?
opts: Correct. Young children and immunocompromised contacts need prompt public-health assessment, because both carry a higher risk of progression, and early infection or immunosuppression can make the first skin test or blood assay falsely negative.
Adult contacts with a negative first test

A negative first test in an adult contact is repeated 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure when indicated. Tell: the contacts flagged for prompt assessment are young children and the immunocompromised.
Prior vaccination affects how a skin test reads, causing false positives, but does not mark a contact for prompt assessment. Tell: priority goes to young children and the immunocompromised.
Adult contacts who have no symptoms

Contacts without symptoms are tested and, if negative early, retested at 8 to 10 weeks; symptoms would prompt disease evaluation now. Tell: the named priority groups are young children and immunocompromised contacts.

set1.q: How long is the shortened regimen for selected children with nonsevere drug-susceptible tuberculosis?
opts: Correct. Selected children with nonsevere tuberculosis can receive 4 months of treatment: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide, with or without ethambutol, then 2 months of isoniazid and rifampin. Eligibility requires expert review.
Six months is the standard regimen: 2 months of four drugs then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin. Tell: the shortened children's option is 4 months.
Nine months of isoniazid alone is an alternative regimen for latent infection when rifamycins are unsuitable. Tell: the shortened children's disease regimen is 4 months.
Twelve months is the minimum course after culture conversion for Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease. Tell: selected children with nonsevere tuberculosis get 4 months.

set1.q: What supports completion of daily tuberculosis therapy?
opts: Correct. Daily therapy with directly observed therapy, in person or by video, supports completion of the standard regimen. Adherence, symptoms and adverse effects are reviewed at least monthly.
Self-report is not what supports completion; directly observed therapy, in person or by video, does. Tell: someone watches the dose being taken.
Sputum cultures are followed until conversion to judge response, not to secure adherence. Tell: completion is supported by directly observed therapy.
Twice-yearly visits fall far short of the monitoring standard: adherence, symptoms and adverse effects are reviewed at least monthly. Tell: daily therapy is supported by direct observation.

set1.q: Why is an interferon-gamma release assay preferred over the tuberculin skin test for most BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin)-vaccinated patients?
opts: The vaccine makes skin tests falsely negative

The vaccine works the other way: it can cause a false-positive tuberculin skin test, as some nontuberculous mycobacterial exposures can. Tell: vaccination pushes the skin test toward positive, which is why the blood assay is preferred.
It separates latent from active disease

Neither the blood assay nor the skin test distinguishes latent infection from tuberculosis disease; a positive result requires clinical evaluation and imaging. Tell: the assay's advantage is about vaccination, not staging.
Its cut-offs are adjusted for vaccine history

The blood assay is not read against induration cut-offs, and the skin test itself is interpreted with standard risk-based thresholds regardless of vaccination history. Tell: nothing is adjusted for the vaccine; the blood assay is simply not made positive by it.
It is not made positive by the vaccine

Correct. BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccination does not cause a positive interferon-gamma release assay, which measures immune responses to tuberculosis-specific antigens, whereas the vaccine can cause a false-positive skin test. The assay is therefore preferred for most vaccinated patients.

Imaging supports suspicion but cannot confirm tuberculosis or reliably determine activity, so films cannot carry monitoring. Tell: response is judged clinically and by sputum culture conversion.

set1.q: Which tests are requested on the sputum specimens in suspected pulmonary tuberculosis?
opts: Correct. Each specimen is sent for an acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, with a rapid molecular test on at least one respiratory specimen and molecular and culture-based drug-susceptibility testing.
The interferon-gamma release assay is a blood test of the immune response to infection, not a sputum test. Tell: sputum goes for smear, culture, molecular and susceptibility testing.
The tuberculin skin test is an intradermal injection read on the forearm at 48 to 72 hours, unrelated to sputum. Tell: sputum looks for the organism, the skin test for an immune response.

Antigen and antibody testing are not part of the tuberculosis sputum workup; sputum is sent for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture plus molecular testing. Tell: the organism is sought directly in the specimen.

set2.q: After the first exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, what usually happens?
opts: Infectious disease soon after the first infection happens only when containment fails, as progressive primary tuberculosis. Tell: the usual course is an immune reaction that holds the infection in check.

Correct. Initial exposure induces an immune reaction that usually quells the infection and confers resistance. The foci can still harbor viable organisms for years, which can reactivate when immunity falls.
Miliary spread to liver and spleen

Massive hematogenous dissemination to the liver and spleen, miliary tuberculosis, follows progressive disease when containment fails, especially with immune compromise. Tell: the usual outcome of a first exposure is containment.
Upper-lobe disease that may cavitate is the post-primary pattern, a later stage. Tell: the first exposure usually ends in containment, not cavitation.

set2.q: Which patient groups may present atypically with pulmonary tuberculosis?
opts: Correct. Children, older adults and immunocompromised patients may present atypically. Examination has limited sensitivity in every group, so symptoms, risk history, imaging and microbiology guide the evaluation.

Diabetes, tobacco use and harmful alcohol use are additional risk factors for progression from infection to disease, not groups named for atypical presentation. Tell: atypical presentation is about age and immune status.

Close contact and travel or residence in high-incidence areas are exposure risks. They say who may be infected, not who presents atypically. Tell: the atypical groups are the very young, the old and the immunocompromised.

Calcified granulomas on imaging may reflect prior infection; they do not define a group that presents atypically. Tell: atypical presentation is named for children, older adults and immunocompromised patients.

set2.q: What may persistent dyspnea after treated tuberculosis reflect?
opts: Breathlessness alone does not mean the patient is infectious; infectiousness depends on pulmonary or laryngeal disease releasing aerosols. Tell: after treatment, persistent dyspnea points to bronchiectasis or other lung injury.

Correct. Persistent dyspnea after tuberculosis may reflect bronchiectasis or other lung injury. Scarring, volume loss or calcified granulomas may remain, and new symptoms require reassessment for recurrence and alternative diagnoses.

Reactivation would bring new symptoms that require reassessment for recurrence; persistent dyspnea after tuberculosis is attributed to bronchiectasis or other lung injury. Tell: lasting breathlessness reflects damage left behind.

A false-negative skin test comes from early infection, immunosuppression or severe disease; it has nothing to do with dyspnea after treatment. Tell: post-tuberculosis dyspnea reflects lung injury such as bronchiectasis.

set2.q: Which setting raises the risk of tuberculosis transmission from an infectious case?
opts: A person with latent infection cannot spread the disease, so sharing a home with one carries no transmission risk from that person. Tell: the source must have infectious pulmonary or laryngeal disease.
ruled out by a stated finding

Extrapulmonary disease such as spinal tuberculosis usually is not infectious unless the lungs or larynx are involved or an aerosol-generating source is present. Tell: risk follows airway disease and shared indoor air.

A contact's positive skin test shows that the contact is infected; it says nothing about the setting's transmission risk. Tell: transmission depends on an infectious source and poorly ventilated shared air.

Correct. Transmission risk increases with prolonged shared indoor air and poor ventilation, and prolonged exposure in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces is a listed exposure risk. Spread is airborne, through aerosols from pulmonary or laryngeal disease.

set2.q: When should a high-risk patient with symptoms that could be pulmonary tuberculosis be evaluated?
opts: Waiting for 3 weeks of cough is exactly what is advised against for a high-risk patient. Tell: high risk plus symptoms means evaluate now.

Eight to 10 weeks after the last exposure is when a negative skin test or blood assay is repeated in a recent contact, not how long to wait with symptoms. Tell: symptoms require disease evaluation now.
Hemoptysis may occur but is not required for a diagnosis, and symptoms may be mild or absent. Tell: the trigger for evaluation is a high-risk patient with symptoms, not a dramatic sign.

Correct. Symptoms may be mild or absent, and a high-risk patient should not wait 3 weeks to be evaluated. Symptoms or high clinical suspicion require evaluation for disease now, using symptoms, risk history, imaging and microbiology.

set2.q: When is a tuberculin skin test read?
opts: Twelve to 24 hours is too early; the reaction is measured by a trained reader at 48 to 72 hours. Tell: the read window opens at 48 hours.
Twenty-four to 48 hours ends where the correct window begins; the reading is made at 48 to 72 hours. Tell: remember 48 to 72.

Correct. In the Mantoux tuberculin skin test, purified protein derivative is injected intradermally on the forearm and a trained reader measures the reaction at 48 to 72 hours, recording the transverse induration in millimeters.
Ninety-six to 120 hours is past the window; the trained reader measures the induration at 48 to 72 hours. Tell: 72 hours is the end of the window.

set2.q: Which group uses a tuberculin skin test induration cut-off of 5 mm or more?
opts: Correct. The 5 mm cut-off applies to human immunodeficiency virus infection, recent close contacts, transplant recipients, major immunosuppression, and imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis.
High-risk congregate settings belong to the 10 mm group, with increased exposure risk, selected medical risks and children under 5. Tell: 5 mm is for contacts and the immunosuppressed.
Children under 5, or children exposed to high-risk adults, use the 10 mm cut-off. Tell: the young child is a 10, the recent close contact is a 5.
With no known tuberculosis risk factors, 15 mm or more is needed for a positive result. Tell: no risk factors means the highest cut-off.

set2.q: What is the role of chest imaging in suspected tuberculosis?
opts: Imaging cannot reliably determine activity. Fibrotic lesions, for example, warrant review of prior treatment and exclusion of active disease. Tell: activity is settled clinically and microbiologically.
Radiographs cannot reliably distinguish recent infection, reactivation or reinfection. Tell: the patterns overlap, so films cannot reliably time the infection.

Correct. Chest radiography is part of the initial evaluation and may show infiltrates, cavities, nodules, adenopathy or effusion. Imaging supports suspicion but cannot confirm tuberculosis or reliably determine activity, so suspected disease goes on to the microbiologic evaluation.
Imaging cannot confirm tuberculosis; it supports suspicion, and the microbiologic evaluation of sputum follows. Tell: the film raises the question, sputum answers it.

set2.q: What tuberculin skin test induration cut-off applies to a child under 5 years of age?
opts: Five millimeters is for human immunodeficiency virus infection, recent close contact, transplant, major immunosuppression or imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. Tell: young age alone puts a child in the 10 mm group.

Correct. Children under 5, or children exposed to high-risk adults, fall in the 10 mm group, with increased exposure risk, selected medical risks and high-risk congregate settings. Young children who are contacts also need prompt public-health assessment.
Fifteen millimeters is for people with no known risk factors, and being under 5 is itself a risk category. Tell: children under 5 read at 10 mm.
There is no 20 mm cut-off; the thresholds are 5, 10 and 15 mm. Tell: a child under 5 is read at 10 mm.

set2.q: At minimum, how often are adherence, symptoms and adverse effects reviewed during tuberculosis treatment?
opts: Weekly review is more often than required; the minimum is a review at least monthly, while directly observed therapy supports daily adherence. Tell: the minimum review interval is monthly.

Correct. Adherence, symptoms and adverse effects are reviewed at least monthly, sputum cultures are followed until conversion, response is documented at 2 months, and liver injury, drug interactions and drug-specific toxicity are monitored.
Every 3 months is too infrequent; adherence, symptoms and adverse effects are reviewed at least monthly. Tell: monthly, not quarterly.
Waiting until the end would miss liver injury, interactions and nonadherence along the way. Tell: the review happens at least monthly during treatment.

set2.q: Where is a hospitalized patient with possible infectious pulmonary tuberculosis placed?
opts: Correct. An airborne infection isolation room is used when indicated, staff wear fit-tested N95 or higher respiratory protection, and the patient uses source control during transport. The local or state tuberculosis program is notified.
Shared room with masks for both
Sharing a room exposes the roommate to airborne aerosols; the patient goes to an airborne infection isolation room when indicated. Tell: transmission rises with shared, poorly ventilated indoor air.

Tuberculosis spreads through infectious aerosols released by coughing, speaking or singing, so the placement is an airborne infection isolation room, with fit-tested N95 or higher protection for staff. Tell: the room must match airborne spread.
Standard ward room with a fan

Transmission risk rises with prolonged shared indoor air and poor ventilation, so an ordinary ward room is not enough; the patient goes to an airborne infection isolation room when indicated. Tell: airborne spread needs an airborne infection isolation room.

set2.q: What does a positive acid-fast smear of sputum establish?
opts: Immune responses to tuberculosis infection are what the tuberculin skin test and the interferon-gamma release assay detect. A smear looks for the organism itself in the specimen. Tell: smear = organism; skin and blood tests = immune response.
A group of organisms, not the species

Correct. An acid-fast smear identifies a group of organisms, the acid-fast bacilli with lipid-rich, mycolic acid cell walls. It does not distinguish Mycobacterium tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria, so culture and molecular testing must name the species.

The smear cannot confirm Mycobacterium tuberculosis, because nontuberculous mycobacteria are acid-fast too. Species identification comes from culture and molecular tests. Tell: a smear names a group of organisms, not the species.

Susceptibility comes from separate molecular and culture-based drug-susceptibility testing ordered on the specimens. The smear only shows that acid-fast bacilli are present. Tell: susceptibility is its own test, not a smear reading.

set2.q: Which condition is listed as an additional risk factor for progression from tuberculosis infection to disease?
opts: Hypertension is not a listed progression risk factor. The listed additional factors include diabetes and chronic kidney disease or dialysis, with silicosis, malnutrition, tobacco and harmful alcohol use. Tell: kidney disease is on the list; blood pressure is not.

BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccination affects how a skin test reads, causing false positives, but it is not a progression risk. Tell: the vaccine changes how the skin test reads; it is not on the progression list.
Correct. The additional progression risk factors are diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease or dialysis, silicosis, low body weight or malnutrition, and tobacco use and harmful alcohol use.

Asthma is not among the tuberculosis progression risk factors. The additional ones are diabetes, chronic kidney disease or dialysis, silicosis, low body weight or malnutrition, tobacco and harmful alcohol use. Tell: silicosis is the lung disease on the list.

set2.q: How many visits does an interferon-gamma release assay need for specimen collection?
opts: Correct. The interferon-gamma release assay is a blood test that needs one visit for specimen collection. A tuberculin skin test, by contrast, must be read by a trained reader at 48 to 72 hours after it is placed.
Two visits describe the skin test pattern, placement then a reading at 48 to 72 hours. The blood assay needs one visit for specimen collection. Tell: blood test, one visit.
Three is the number of sputum specimens collected for suspected pulmonary disease, not blood-assay visits. Tell: the blood assay needs one visit.
Four visits has no basis; the blood assay needs one visit for specimen collection. Tell: a single blood draw is its convenience over the skin test.

set2.q: Which form of tuberculosis releases infectious aerosols during coughing, speaking or singing?
opts: Spinal tuberculosis is extrapulmonary disease, which usually is not infectious unless pulmonary or laryngeal involvement or an aerosol-generating source is present. Tell: the airway sites spread it.
Lymph node disease, with persistent, often painless enlargement, is extrapulmonary and usually not infectious. Tell: disease of the airway, pulmonary or laryngeal, is the usual source of aerosols.

Correct. Pulmonary and laryngeal tuberculosis can release infectious aerosols during coughing, speaking or singing. Extrapulmonary disease usually is not infectious unless the lungs or larynx are involved or an aerosol-generating source is present.
Latent tuberculosis infection does not cause transmission: the person is infected but has no disease and cannot spread it. Tell: aerosols need pulmonary or laryngeal disease.

set2.q: What must be done before starting treatment for latent tuberculosis infection?
opts: A positive result is not repeated; it requires clinical evaluation and chest imaging to look for disease. Tell: the step before latent treatment is excluding disease.
A negative assay would argue against infection, not prepare for latent treatment; the skin test and blood assay may stay positive after treatment anyway. Tell: the requirement is excluding disease.
Symptoms would point to disease, which needs evaluation now and a different regimen. Tell: latent treatment starts only after disease has been excluded.

Correct. Tuberculosis disease is excluded before latent treatment begins, because a positive skin test or blood assay shows infection but cannot separate latent infection from disease. Interactions, pregnancy and source-case resistance are also checked.

set2.q: When are 6 or 9 months of isoniazid alone used for latent tuberculosis infection?
opts: Correct. The 6H or 9H (6 or 9 months of isoniazid) regimens are alternatives when rifamycin regimens are unsuitable. The preferred short regimens are weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months, daily rifampin for 4 months, and daily isoniazid plus rifampin for 3 months.
Isoniazid alone is the alternative, not the preferred choice; the preferred regimens are the short rifamycin-based ones. Tell: long isoniazid is for when rifamycins cannot be used.
Disease must be excluded before any latent regimen starts. Tell: latent treatment, of any length, follows the exclusion of disease.
The weekly option is isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months. Tell: 6 or 9 months of isoniazid replaces the rifamycin regimens when they are unsuitable.

set2.q: Which condition is on the differential for pulmonary tuberculosis as another cause of cavitary lung disease?
opts: Acute bronchitis is not on the tuberculosis differential. The cavitary competitors are lung abscess, nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, chronic pulmonary aspergillosis and lung cancer. Tell: cancer is named among the causes of cavitary disease.

Asthma is not on the pulmonary tuberculosis differential, which lists infections, bronchiectasis, chronic pulmonary aspergillosis and lung cancer. Tell: fever, weight loss and hemoptysis point toward the listed causes, cancer among them.

Pneumothorax is not on the pulmonary tuberculosis differential. Lung cancer and other causes of cavitary disease are. Tell: the differential is built around cough, weight loss, hemoptysis and cavities.

Correct. The differential for pulmonary tuberculosis includes nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, bacterial pneumonia or lung abscess, endemic fungal infection including histoplasmosis, bronchiectasis or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, and lung cancer and other causes of cavitary disease.

set2.q: Which statement about hemoptysis in pulmonary tuberculosis is accurate?
opts: It usually points to another diagnosis
Hemoptysis is a listed manifestation of pulmonary tuberculosis, though fever, weight loss and hemoptysis also have a broad differential. Tell: it fits tuberculosis; it just does not prove it.
Hemoptysis is a pulmonary manifestation; extrapulmonary disease shows organ findings such as painless node enlargement, effusion, headache or back pain. Tell: blood in the sputum comes from the lung.
It may occur but is not required

Correct. Hemoptysis or pleuritic chest pain may occur, but dramatic hemoptysis is not required for a diagnosis. The manifestations are persistent cough, fever and night sweats, and weight loss, reduced appetite and fatigue, and symptoms may be mild or absent.
It is usually needed for the diagnosis
Dramatic hemoptysis is not required for a diagnosis of tuberculosis, and symptoms may be mild or absent. Tell: the absence of hemoptysis does not exclude the disease.

set2.q: Reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis most often follows which circumstance in a person with latent infection?
opts: A healed lesion holds organisms that are not viable, so healing is the opposite of the path to reactivation. Tell: reactivation needs dormant, viable organisms in a latent lesion.
The skin test measures an immune response to infection; it does not trigger reactivation. Tell: diminished immunity, not a test result, lets a latent focus reactivate.

Correct. Reactivation tuberculosis is latent infection that progresses to disease, often with impaired immunity. Foci of the first infection can harbor viable bacilli for years and reactivate in states of diminished immunity.
A new exposure to a case
A fresh exposure that causes a new infection is reinfection, which is a separate event from reactivation. Tell: reactivation comes from organisms already dormant in the person.

set2.q: What does rifampin resistance require?
opts: Ethambutol is already in the standard initial phase; rifampin resistance instead requires rapid susceptibility testing and expert management. Tell: resistance goes to experts, with rapid susceptibility testing.
Lengthening the standard regimen does not address resistance; resistance to a key drug requires rapid susceptibility testing and expert management. Tell: extend nothing on your own; call the experts.
Four months of daily rifampin is a latent infection regimen, and it cannot work against rifampin-resistant organisms. Tell: rifampin resistance sends the patient to expert care.

Correct. Rifampin resistance requires rapid susceptibility testing and expert management. Drug-susceptibility testing, molecular and culture-based, is obtained at diagnosis so that resistance is found early.

set2.q: What do calcified granulomas on a chest film suggest?
opts: Miliary disease produces diffuse tiny nodules from hematogenous spread, not calcified granulomas. Tell: calcification is the mark of an old, healed focus.
Calcified granulomas reflect prior infection; infectiousness depends on current pulmonary or laryngeal disease releasing aerosols. Tell: calcium in a granuloma looks backward, not at today's risk.
Upper-lobe disease that may cavitate is the post-primary pattern of active disease. Tell: calcified granulomas, scarring and volume loss are the signs of prior infection.

Correct. Scarring, volume loss or calcified granulomas may reflect prior infection. Fibrotic lesions warrant review of prior treatment and exclusion of active disease, and latent infection usually has a normal chest radiograph.

set2.q: Which condition raises the risk of nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease?
opts: Recent close contact with a case

Close contact with an infectious case is a tuberculosis exposure risk; nontuberculous infection rarely spreads person to person. Tell: the nontuberculous risks are structural lung disease and immune dysfunction.

BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccination causes false-positive skin tests; it is not a nontuberculous risk factor. Tell: bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and immune dysfunction raise the risk.
Travel to a high-incidence area is a tuberculosis exposure risk. Tell: nontuberculous lung disease follows damaged airways and immune dysfunction, not travel.

set2.q: Which statement about transmission from a person with latent tuberculosis infection is accurate?
opts: It cannot later progress to contagious disease

Latent infection can progress to tuberculosis disease, often with impaired immunity, and pulmonary or laryngeal disease is then infectious. Tell: latent infection is not contagious now, but it can become disease later.
Contacts cannot catch it from this person

Correct. Latent tuberculosis infection does not cause transmission: the person is infected but asymptomatic and cannot spread the disease. Infectious aerosols come from pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis disease during coughing, speaking or singing.
Household contacts are at risk of spread
Household spread needs infectious pulmonary or laryngeal disease releasing aerosols. Latent infection releases none. Tell: a latent case is not a source of spread.
It stays contagious until treatment ends
Latent infection is not infectious before, during or after treatment, so there is no contagious period to wait out. Tell: latent infection does not cause transmission at any point.
